clue.text: Do members of them call each other "mates," which is wrong?

definitions.text: Do members of them call each other "mates," which is wrong?

indicators.note: the word in quotation marks is wrong as it stands, so its letters must be put right by rearranging them

parts.note: the quoted word is used as written, its letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about whether players on the same side really ought to call each other mates.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the quoted word, rearranged, gives the groups whose members do call each other teammates.
explanation.definitionFit: Players in sports sides commonly call one another teammates, so the groups in question are sports sides.

clue.text: The Australian bird and a ruffled teal imitate a good example.

parts.note: the emu is the large flightless bird of Australia

indicators.note: ruffled feathers are disordered, so the letters of the duck's name are disordered too

parts.note: the duck's name is used as written, as the letters to be ruffled

explanation.surface: An emu and a duck with ruffled feathers copy some admirable model.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate is to copy someone admired in the hope of matching or surpassing them.

clue.text: A city in Germany made around a large number, with common food coming up.

indicators.note: the word made is placed around the large number, enclosing it

parts.note: the word made is used as written, opened up to take in a letter
G stands for a grand, a thousand

indicators.note: in a down answer, coming up means the food word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: grub is a common, slangy word for food

explanation.surface: A German city built around a big population, with ordinary food arriving.
explanation.walkthrough: G is short for grand, a thousand, which makes it the large number; in a down clue the food is written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Magdeburg is a historic city on the Elbe, capital of the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

clue.text: The Egyptian judge of the dead, returning so with the flower?

definitions.text: The Egyptian judge of the dead

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so the little word so is read backwards

parts.note: the little word so is used as written, then turned round
the iris is a garden flower

explanation.surface: A question whether the Egyptian god of the dead comes back with a flower in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: In Egyptian mythology Osiris presided over the underworld and weighed the hearts of the dead.

clue.text: The mouselike insectivore would be wily, if it had 500!

indicators.note: the clue says the creature would become the wily word if it had the extra letter, so that letter must come off the wily word

parts.note: shrewd means clever and canny, a near synonym of wily
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A playful aside: give the little creature five hundred and it would turn cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: the answer plus D makes a word for wily, so remove D from that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrews are tiny, mouse-like mammals that live mainly on insects and worms.

clue.text: What you may do to motor at the lake–or is it just a dream?

parts.words: What you may do to motor
parts.note: you rev a motor, running the engine up fast
Lake Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes

explanation.surface: Pondering whether running a boat engine on the lake is real or just imagined.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a daydream, a state of pleasant absorbed musing.

clue.text: Extreme cruelty makes this unhappy miss lose a point, in confusion.

parts.note: sad is a plain synonym of unhappy

indicators.note: the remaining letters are thrown into confusion, that is rearranged
the word miss is to lose one compass point letter

parts.note: the word miss is used as written before losing a letter
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Someone's terrible cruelty upsets a young woman, who grows muddled and loses her argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadism is taking pleasure in inflicting pain, which is cruelty at its extreme.

clue.text: The people who work for you show something with a flag on it.

definitions.text: The people who work for you
definitions.meaning: first meaning: employees, the personnel of an organisation

definitions.text: something with a flag on it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a pole, as in flagstaff, from which a flag flies

explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both an employer's workforce and the pole a flag is hoisted on.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the employees of a firm and a pole, as used in flagstaff.

clue.text: In a crazy way, Pa's mate shows a manner characteristic to a particular language.

definitions.text: a manner characteristic to a particular language
definitions.note: a noun phrase describing an adverb: the answer means in such a manner

parts.note: idiotically means foolishly, as a crazy person might act
Pa's partner is Ma

explanation.surface: Mum, acting oddly, speaks in a way that sounds just like a native of some tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Ma sits inside the word for crazily, after its first four letters; the clue gives no separate signal for the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically means using the natural turns of phrase native to one language.

clue.text: The latest gossip shows just how the natives speak!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what everyone is currently talking about
second meaning, taken literally: the way its residents talk

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning reads the phrase literally, as the speech of a town's own people.
explanation.definitionFit: The talk of the town is the subject everybody is chatting about; read literally it is the local speech.

clue.text: Ted, strung out over a drug problem, took a long, hard slog.

indicators.note: Ted is stretched out so that it spans the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: the name Ted is used as written, its letters spread around the rest

indicators.note: the word drug is a problem to be worked out, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word drug is used as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Ted, high and struggling with addiction, slowly dragged himself through a long ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strung out' and 'drug problem' both point to addiction in the surface; in the wordplay they mean stretched around and rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To trudge is to walk slowly and heavily, so trudged describes a weary, laborious march.

clue.text: Attained fame and success with the District Attorney briefly jumping back over a turbulent river.

indicators.note: the reversed letters sit over, that is around, the rearranged river
the short form jumps back to front, so its two letters are reversed

parts.note: DA is the short form of District Attorney, the US prosecutor

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so the letters of river are churned

parts.note: the word river is used as written as the letters to churn

explanation.surface: Someone became famous by leaping back across rough water alongside a prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: To have arrived is an idiom for having reached success and recognition.

clue.text: The skeleton seems to deliberately get one in trouble, on the job.

parts.note: to frame someone is to fabricate evidence against them
at work means on the job

explanation.surface: A skeleton apparently sets someone up deliberately while at work.
explanation.definitionFit: A framework is a supporting structure, which is what a skeleton is to a body.

clue.text: See 27
Ordinary troops. (As a matter of custom, makes you do something!)

parts.note: regular means habitual, done as a matter of custom
forces means compels

explanation.surface: A note on standard soldiers: habit itself can compel you to act.
explanation.definitionFit: Regular forces are the standing professional army, as opposed to reservists or irregular militia.

clue.text: A sort of carpet to eat on–but they're not exactly the winning type!

definitions.text: they're not exactly the winning type

parts.note: a runner is a long narrow rug for a hall or stairs
to sup is to take supper, to eat

explanation.surface: A rug to dine on, followed by a dig at people who never quite win.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners-up finish just behind the winner, so they are close to winning but not winners.

clue.text: A shopper looking for a good deal at the drinking spot, to win one out for the game…

definitions.text: A shopper looking for a good deal

parts.note: a bar is a place to drink
to gain is to win or obtain
a hunter goes out after game, wild animals hunted for food or sport

explanation.surface: A deal-seeker at the bar, hoping to win something at a game, with the scene running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a pub game to win, but it is quarry: the hunter is out after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain hunter shops around seeking goods at low prices.

clue.text: Take little notice, a sort of turn is dead–but you really like things this way!

definitions.text: you really like things this way

parts.note: an ad is a short advertisement, a small notice
a U-turn, identified by its letter
the late someone is someone who has died

explanation.surface: A paradox: ignore something, accept a death, and yet claim you love it this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take little notice' suggests ignoring; it is a small advertisement. The definition loosely describes praising things to excess.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulate is to admire or flatter extravagantly, which is how you treat what you dote on.

clue.text: Crazy bone comes with it, to a point, but it makes combs and buttons appear.

definitions.text: it makes combs and buttons appear

indicators.note: the word bone goes crazy, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: the word bone is used as written as the letters to scramble
taken as written
E, east, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A funny bone, sharpened to a point, somehow produces combs and buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy bone' is the American name for the funny bone, but here crazy just scrambles the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebonite is hard vulcanised rubber, long used for moulding combs, buttons and pipe stems.

clue.text: A sort of support when the last month comes up short, but prepared for anything.

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment

indicators.note: in a down answer, coming up means the month's letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: December is the last month; short refers to its abbreviation

explanation.surface: Some support, and the year running out, yet someone remains ready for whatever comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' signals the abbreviation of December rather than a shortfall.
explanation.definitionFit: To be braced is to be steeled and ready for an impact or a shock.

clue.text: You've got to make counterfeits for George, see?

indicators.note: the clue invites you to look at the words for George, where the answer can be seen in plain view

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of for into the start of the name George

explanation.surface: Instructions to fake documents on someone's behalf.
explanation.definitionFit: To forge is to make an illegal copy, such as a counterfeit banknote or signature.

clue.text: …with drinks served to everyone.

parts.note: continuing the previous clue's pub scene, it sounds like drinking at a game
the setter's sense: a set of drinks bought for everyone in the group

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on the bar scene of the clue before; the answer is a set of drinks bought for the whole company.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying a round means ordering one drink for each person in the party.

clue.text: And the same to you!

parts.note: the retort reads like a rude reply to an insult
the setter's sense: the word used to say the same again

explanation.walkthrough: The retort sounds like a riposte; the answer is the word that says 'the same again'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto means the same thing again, used to agree or echo what was just said.

clue.text: A city in Massachusetts, with the start of the fight lost, and you get to steal back with nothing.

indicators.note: points to the first letter of the fight word
that first letter is lost, dropped from the word

parts.note: a battle is a fight

indicators.note: the stealing word goes back, read in reverse

parts.note: to rob is to steal

explanation.surface: Losing the opening of a brawl in a Massachusetts city, so you sneak back empty-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: Attleboro is a small city in Bristol County, south-eastern Massachusetts, once famed for jewellery making.

clue.text: Have a little talk, and let back what should belong to you.

parts.note: to chat is to talk informally

indicators.note: the word let is set back, written in reverse

parts.note: the word let is used as written, then turned back

explanation.surface: Talk it over, and let back in what is rightfully yours.
explanation.definitionFit: A chattel is an item of movable personal property, something that belongs to its owner.

clue.text: It gnaws madly, which is wrecking a body's health!

indicators.note: the letters of the two words act madly, scrambled into a new order

parts.note: the two words are used as written, their seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something gnawing away like crazy, ruining a person's health.
explanation.definitionFit: A wasting disease makes the body thin and weak, gradually destroying health.

clue.text: What the bird lives on suggests a council in 1521.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: a bird's food
second meaning: the imperial assembly at ..., Germany, before which Martin Luther was tried in 1521

explanation.walkthrough: A diet here is a formal assembly; Worms is a German city on the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Diet of Worms was the 1521 imperial assembly that condemned Luther; read literally it is food for birds.

clue.text: Bring back the wide oceans, poetically–and hurry up!

indicators.note: the poetic word is brought back, read in reverse

parts.note: the deeps is a poetic name for the sea

explanation.surface: A poet's urgent plea to restore the vast seas, and quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To speed is to go faster, the same as to hurry up.
